name: Loaded framing
what: marks an intensifier or evaluatively charged term from the English pack
affordance: can make an evaluation or frame salient through the vocabulary itself
mechanism: evaluative redescription: every word evokes a frame, and negating a frame activates it (Lakoff); frames shift judgment even about events people watched themselves
benign_reading: Vivid language is not a crime, and naming a wrong plainly ('this was theft') can be precision, not spin. The tell is emotion doing the work an argument should do.
ledger_line: {n} intensifier or evaluatively charged term{s} matched
output_phrasing: this span contains an intensifier or evaluatively charged term from the English pack

specimens.quote: And with all due respect, the fact is we had four dead Americans. Was it because of a protest or was it because of guys out for a walk one night who decided they would go kill some Americans? What difference, at this point, does it make?
specimens.speaker: Hillary Clinton, U.S. Secretary of State

specimens.quote: Our company was dishonest, with the EPA and the California Air Resources board, and with all of you and in my German words, we have totally screwed up.
specimens.speaker: Michael Horn, President and CEO, Volkswagen Group of America
specimens.note: The folksy intensifier performs maximal candor while reframing years of engineered defeat-device fraud as a blunder — 'totally screwed up' sounds more contrite than 'cheated' while admitting less.

specimens.quote: This is clearly a disappointing event for our company, and one that strikes at the heart of who we are and what we do.
specimens.speaker: Richard F. Smith, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Equifax Inc.
specimens.note: 'Clearly' imports agreed-upon obviousness onto the euphemism 'disappointing event', grading a breach of 143 million people's data as a mood — and casting the company, not consumers, as the injured party.

specimens.quote: So we're going to be signing today, and registering, national emergency. And it's a great thing to do because we have an invasion of drugs, invasion of gangs, invasion of people, and it's unacceptable.
specimens.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
specimens.note: 'Invasion', repeated three times, imports a military frame that makes the emergency feel self-evident by vocabulary alone — the loaded noun does the work the contested legal justification was being asked to do.

specimens.quote: I want to be clear at the outset: any allegation that Robinhood acted to help hedge funds or other special interests to the detriment of our customers is absolutely false and market-distorting rhetoric.
specimens.speaker: Vladimir Tenev, co-founder and CEO, Robinhood Markets, Inc.
specimens.note: 'Absolutely false' plus the counter-label 'market-distorting rhetoric' delegitimizes the accusers before any evidence is weighed — intensity and name-calling stand in for the account of why buying was halted.

citations: Lakoff, G. (2004). Don't Think of an Elephant!

honest_twins.text: Make no mistake: the spillway is cracked, and the inspection report says it will not survive another flood season. Close the road below the dam today.
honest_twins.note: The same preemptive intensifier is honest here because the urgency is earned and argued in the same breath — a checkable inspection report carries the claim, so the emotion matches the stakes instead of substituting for evidence.

honest_twins.text: The fact is this invoice was paid twice — here are both bank statements, dated three weeks apart.
honest_twins.note: 'The fact is' introduces something that actually is a documented fact, with the receipts attached in the same sentence; per the entry's benign reading, naming a wrong plainly is precision, because an argument — not the loaded frame — is doing the work.
